title: God does not leave his seat
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦθ᾿ ὁ γενναιότατος Κέλσος οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὁπόθεν λαβὼν ἐπαπορεῖ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ὡς λέγοντας ὅτι αὐτὸς κάτεισι πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ὁ θεός· καὶ οἴεται ἀκολουθεῖν τούτῳ τὸ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἕδραν αὐτὸν καταλιπεῖν. οὐ γὰρ οἶδε δύναμιν θεοῦ καὶ „ὅτι πνεῦμα κυρίου πεπλήρωκε τὴν οἰκουμένην, καὶ τὸ συνέχον τὰ πάντα γνῶσιν ἔχει φωνῆς,“ οὐδὲ συνιέναι δύναται τὸ „οὐχὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν ἐγὼ πληρῶ; λέγει κύριος,“ οὐδὲ βλέπει ὅτι κατὰ τὸν Χριστιανῶν λόγον οἱ πάντες „ἐν αὐτῷ ζῶμεν καὶ κινούμεθα καὶ ἐσμὲν,“ ὡς καὶ Παῦλος ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους δημηγορίᾳ ἐδίδαξε. κἂν ὁ θεὸς τοίνυν τῶν ὅλων τῇ ἑαυτοῦ δυνάμει συγκαταβαίνῃ τῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον, κἂν ὁ „ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν“ λόγος. „θεὸς“ καὶ αὐτὸς ὢν, ἔρχηται πρὸς ἡμᾶς. οὐκ ἔξεδρος γίνεται οὐδὲ καταλείπει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἕδραν. ὡς τινὰ μὲν τόπον κενὸν αὐτοῦ εἶναι ἕτερον δὲ πλήρη, οὐ πρότερον αὐτὸν ἔχοντα. ἐπιδημεῖ δὲ δύναμις καὶ θειότης θεοῦ δι᾿ οὗ βούλεται καὶ ἐν ᾧ εὑρίσκει χώραν. οὐκ ἀμείβοντος τόπον οὐδ᾿ ἐκλείποντος χώραν αὐτοῦ κενὴν καὶ ἄλλην πληροῦντος. ἵνα γὰρ καὶ ἐκλείπειν αὐτὸν φῶμεν καὶ ἄλλον τινὰ πληροῦν, οὐ περὶ τόπου τὸ τοιοῦτον ἀποφανούμεθα· ἀλλὰ τὴν μὲν τοῦ φαύλου καὶ κεχυμένου ἐν τῇ κακίᾳ ψυχὴν φήσομεν καταλείπεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, τὴν δὲ τοῦ βουλομένου ζῆν κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἢ καὶ προκόπτοντος ἢ καὶ ἤδη ζῶντος κατ᾿ αὐτὴν ἀποφανούμεθα πληροῦσθαι ἢ μετέχειν θείου πνεύματος. οὐ χρεία οὖν εἰς τὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ κάθοδον ἢ εἰς τὴν πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἐπιστροφὴν τοῦ θεοῦ καταλείπεσθαι ἕδραν μείζονα καὶ μεταβάλλεσθαι τὰ τῇδε, ὡς ὁ Κέλσος οἴεται, λέγων· εἰ γὰρ ἕν τι τῶν τῇδε τοὐλάχιστον μεταβάλοις, ἀνατραπέντα οἰχήσεταί σοι τὰ πάντα. εἰ δὲ χρὴ λέγειν μεταβάλλειν παρουσίᾳ δυνάμεως θεοῦ καὶ ἐπιδημίᾳ τοῦ λόγου εἰς ἀνθρώπους τινὰ, οὐκ ὀκνήσομεν λέγειν μεταβάλλειν ἐκ φαύλου εἰς ἀστεῖον καὶ ἐξ ἀκολάστου εἰς σώφρονα καὶ ἐκ δεισιδαίμονος εἰς εὐσεβῆ τὸν παραδεξάμενον τὴν τοῦ λόγου τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπιδημίαν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things the most noble (γενναιότατος, ironic) Celsus, taking [it] I know not from where, raises a difficulty (ἐπαπορέω) against us as [if we were] saying that God himself comes down (κάτειμι) to men; and he thinks there follows (ἀκολουθέω) on this that he leaves (καταλείπω) his own seat (ἕδρα). For he does not know the power (δύναμις) of God and 'that the Spirit (πνεῦμα) of the Lord has filled (πληρόω) the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη), and that which holds together (συνέχω) all things has knowledge (γνῶσις) of voice/speech (φωνή)', nor can he understand (συνίημι) the [saying] 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord', nor does he see that according to the word (λόγος) of Christians we all 'in him live (ζάω) and move (κινέομαι) and are (εἰμί)', as Paul too taught in the public speech (δημηγορία) to the Athenians. So even if the God of the whole (ὁ θεὸς τῶν ὅλων) by his own power comes down together (συγκαταβαίνω) with Jesus into the life (βίος) of men, even if the Word (λόγος) [who was] 'in the beginning (ἀρχή) with God', being himself also 'God', comes to us, he does not become out of his seat (ἔξεδρος) nor leave his own seat, so that some place (τόπος) is empty (κενός) of him and another full (πλήρης), not having him before. But the power and divinity (θειότης) of God sojourns/comes to dwell (ἐπιδημέω) through whom he/it wills (βούλομαι) and in whom it finds (εὑρίσκω) room (χώρα), [God] not exchanging (ἀμείβω) place nor leaving (ἐκλείπω) his space empty and filling another. For even if we say that he leaves and fills some other, we will not declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) such a thing about place; but the soul of the worthless (φαῦλος) and poured out/dissipated (χέω, perf. pass.) in vice (κακία) we will say is forsaken (καταλείπω, pass.) by God, but [the soul] of one wishing to live according to virtue (ἀρετή), or also progressing (προκόπτω), or also already living according to it, we will declare is filled or shares in (μετέχω) the divine Spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα). There is no need then, for the descent (κάθοδος) of Christ or for the turning (ἐπιστροφή) of God toward men, that a greater (μείζων) seat be left and the things here be changed (μεταβάλλω), as Celsus thinks, saying: 'For if you change one, the least (τοὐλάχιστον), of the things here, overturned (ἀνατρέπω) all things will be gone (οἴχομαι) for you.' But if it is necessary to say that someone changes by presence (παρουσία) of the power of God and by coming (ἐπιδημία) of the Word to men, we will not hesitate (ὀκνέω) to say that he changes from worthless (φαῦλος) to good/refined (ἀστεῖος), and from licentious (ἀκόλαστος) to self-controlled (σώφρων), and from superstitious (δεισιδαίμων) to pious (εὐσεβής), the one who received (παραδέχομαι) the coming of the Word of God into his own soul.
pass_b_english: After this the most noble Celsus, taking it from I know not where, raises a difficulty against us, as though we said that God himself comes down to men; and he thinks it follows from this that he leaves his own seat. For he does not know the power of God, nor that “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of what is spoken” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:7). Nor can he understand the words, “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24). Nor does he see that, according to the Christians’ teaching, “in him we all live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28), as Paul too taught in his speech to the Athenians.

So even if the God of the universe, by his own power, comes down with Jesus into the life of men, and even if the Word who was “in the beginning with God,” and who is himself “God” (John 1:1–2), comes to us, he is not displaced, nor does he leave his own seat, as though one place were empty of him and another, which did not have him before, were full. The power and divinity of God comes to dwell through whom he wills and in whom it finds room, while he neither changes place nor leaves his own place empty and fills another.

For even if we should say that he leaves one and fills another, we shall not be declaring this about place. Rather, we shall say that the soul of the wicked man, dissipated in vice, is forsaken by God, while we shall declare that the soul of one who wishes to live according to virtue, or is making progress, or already lives according to it, is filled with the divine Spirit or shares in it.

There is no need, then, for the descent of Christ, or for God’s turning toward men, that a greater seat be left behind and the things here be changed, as Celsus thinks when he says: “For if you were to change even one thing here, the very least, everything would be overturned and gone.” But if we must speak of anyone being changed by the presence of God’s power and the coming of the Word to men, we shall not hesitate to say that whoever has received the coming of the Word of God into his own soul is changed from wicked to good, from licentious to self-controlled, and from superstitious to reverent.

choices.choice: ‘he is not put out of his seat’ → ‘he is not displaced’ (ἔξεδρος γίνεται; ‘put out’ implied an outside agent)

Celsus’s line: ‘you will see everything overturned and gone’ → ‘if you were to change even one thing here, the very least, everything would be overturned and gone’ (‘see’ was not in the Greek; μεταβάλοις is optative; ἕν τι … τοὐλάχιστον kept)
Checked Wisdom of Solomon 1:7, Jeremiah 23:24 (LXX numbering agrees), Acts 17:28, John 1:1–2 against the verses

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 5 (Koetschau 4.5). Celsus’s claim that God would leave his seat is reported indirectly, so it has no quotation marks; his closing sentence (εἰ γὰρ ἕν τι τῶν τῇδε τοὐλάχιστον μεταβάλοις …) is in his own words and is quoted. Wisdom of Solomon 1:7 matches the LXX (πνεῦμα κυρίου πεπλήρωκεν τὴν οἰκουμένην, καὶ τὸ συνέχον τὰ πάντα γνῶσιν ἔχει φωνῆς); γνῶσιν ἔχει φωνῆς rendered ‘has knowledge of what is spoken’. Jeremiah 23:24 matches the LXX; LXX and English numbering agree for this chapter. Acts 17:28 is from Paul’s speech on the Areopagus (Acts 17:22–31), as Origen says. ‘In the beginning with God … God’ draws on John 1:1–2. ‘Power and divinity’ (δύναμις καὶ θειότης) may echo Romans 1:20 (ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης); possible only, not cited inline. The genitive participles ἀμείβοντος … ἐκλείποντος … πληροῦντος agree with θεοῦ, so the English makes God (‘he’) their subject. κεχυμένου ἐν τῇ κακίᾳ (literally ‘poured out in vice’) rendered ‘dissipated in vice’. θείου πνεύματος is God’s Spirit, so capitalised. In the last sentence μεταβάλλειν is taken as intransitive with τὸν παραδεξάμενον as its subject (‘whoever has received … is changed’). The staged text has several stray full stops (after λόγος, ἡμᾶς, ἕδραν and χώραν); the sentences are read as continuous.
